BILL NUMBER:  S1624

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the vehicle and traffic law, in relation to the
operation of an emergency vehicle without a commercial drivers license


 PURPOSE/SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

This bill amends subparagraph (i) of paragraph (d) of subdivision 2 of
section 501 of the New York State Vehicle and Traffic law to delete
provisions which currently prohibit anyone without a commercial
driver's license from driving emergency vehicles.

Adoption of this bill would permit volunteer service responders who
have class "d" licenses to operate emergency vehicles at anytime.

 EXISTING LAW :
Chapter 60 of the laws of 2005 inadvertently amended sections 501 and
501a of the state Vehicle and Traffic law to explicitly carve out
return trips from emergencies in the definition of "emergency
operation."

 JUSTIFICATION :
The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration allows each state to
provide a waiver for commercial drivers' license requirement for first
responders. Historically, New York State statute has provided this
waiver to allow firefighters in the State of New York to operate fire
vehicles with class D licenses. However, chapter 60 of the laws of
2005 amended this statue to prohibit emergency service responders with
class D licenses from operating emergency vehicles after the emergency
in question has concluded.

The 2005 amendment to the law presents a rather awkward situation
where a first responder drives a fire vehicle to the scene of an
emergency and after its conclusion, is forced to deliberately disobey
the law so that they can return the truck to the firehouse. One can
easily imagine a situation where an accident occurs on the return trip
with another vehicle and the volunteer is liable because, pursuant to
current law, they never should have been driving said emergency
vehicle to begin with. The bill would remove this loophole so that our
emergency responders are no longer put in situations where they are
unable to answer calls because no volunteer can drive the equipment
back following the call. The bill would also provide authority for use
of fire apparatus, without CDLs, for things such as, but not limited
to, drills, training, fire inspection, public education, public events
and maintenance.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS :
None.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
Immediately.

B.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S1624B

 TITLE OF BILL :
An act to amend the vehicle and traffic law, in relation to emergency
vehicles and their operation without a commercial drivers license


 PURPOSE SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :
This bill amends subparagraph (i) of paragraph (d) of subdivision 2 of
section 501 of the New York State Vehicle and Traffic law to delete
provisions which currently prohibit anyone without a commercial
driver's license from driving emergency vehicles.

The bill would also amend the opening paragraph of section 115-a of
the vehicle and traffic law to require emergency vehicles to also be
equipped with audible and visual signals and not be subject to normal
traffic regulations in order to comply with Federal Motor Carrier
Safety Regulations ("FMCSRs").

Adoption of this bill would permit volunteer service responders who
have class "d" licenses to operate emergency vehicles when acting
pursuant to his or her official duties.

 EXISTING LAW :
The Transportation and Economic Development ("TEDE") budget bill
included Article 7 language to permit volunteer emergency service
responders to operate emergency vehicles on return from emergency
calls.  The new language did not, however, allow for operation of such
vehicles for training, maintenance, or other times when such trucks
are used for ancillary purposes related to the position.

Prior, chapter 60 of the laws of 2005 inadvertently amended sections
501 and SOla of the state Vehicle and Traffic law to explicitly carve
out return trips from emergencies in the definition of "emergency
operation."

 JUSTIFICATION :
The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration allows each state to
provide a waiver for commercial drivers' license requirement for first
responders. Historically, New York State statute has provided this
waiver to allow firefighters in the State of New York to operate fire
vehicles with class D licenses. However, chapter 60 of the laws of
2005 amended this statue to prohibit emergency service responders with
class D licenses from operating emergency vehicles after the emergency
in question has concluded.

The 2005 amendment to the law presents a rather awkward situation
where a first responder drives a fire vehicle to the scene of an
emergency and after its conclusion, is forced to deliberately disobey
the law so that they can return the truck to the firehouse. One can
easily imagine a situation where an accident occurs on the return trip
with another vehicle and the volunteer is liable because, pursuant to
current law, they never should have been driving said emergency
vehicle to begin with. The bill would remove this loophole so that our
emergency responders are no longer put in situations where they are
unable to answer calls because no volunteer can drive the equipment
back following the call. The bill would also provide authority for use
of fire apparatus, without CDLs, for things such as, but not limited
to, drills, training, fire inspection, public education, public events
and maintenance.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS :
None.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
Immediately.

C.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S1624C

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the vehicle and traffic law, in relation to the
operation of an emergency vehicle without a commercial drivers license


 PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL :

To clarify the scope of the exemption from commercial driver's license
(CDL) requirements applicable to the operation of certain emergency
vehicles.

 SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS :

The bill amends subparagraph (i) of paragraph (d) of subdivision 2 of
Section 501, and paragraph (b) of subdivision 4 of Section 501-a of
the Vehicle and Traffic Law to clarify that the current exemption from
CDL requirements for police vehicles, fire vehicles and vehicles used
to provide emergency medical service applies not only during their use
in emergency situations but also in the performance of official
duties, or activities related to the execution of emergency
governmental functions.

 JUSTIFICATION :

Regulations promulgated by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety
Administration (FMCSA) authorize states, in their discretion, to
exempt from CDL requirements firefighters and other operators of
commercial motor vehicles which are necessary to the preservation of
life or property or to the execution of emergency governmental
functions (49 CFR 383.3(d)), that are equipped with audible and visual
signals and not subject to normal traffic regulation during emergency
situations.

Current New York State law exempts from CDL requirements, in emergency
situations, police vehicles, fire vehicles and vehicles used to
provide emergency medical service. These vehicles, which are included
in the definition of "authorized emergency vehicle" in Vehicle and
Traffic Law (VTL) §101, are subject to the provisions of VTL §1104
when engaged in an emergency operation. This section sets forth
standards for the operation of authorized emergency vehicles engaged
in emergency operations including provisions for lights, sirens, and
exemption from normal traffic regulation.

The operators of such vehicles are restricted by current statutory
definition. For example, pursuant to VTL §132-a, a vehicle is a police
vehicle only if it is owned by the state, a public authority, a
county, town, city or village, and operated by the police department
or law enforcement agency of such governmental unit or by a constable
or police constable of a town when acting pursuant to his special
duties. As another example, pursuant to VTL §115-a, a vehicle is a
fire vehicle if it is  OPERATED FOR FIRE SERVICE PURPOSES  and owned
and identified as being owned by the state, a public authority, a
county, town, city, village or fire district, or a fire corporation
subject to provisions of the not-for-profit corporation law or a fire
company as defined in § 100 of the General Municipal Law.

This bill would clarify, in a manner conforming to federal regulations
and thereby preserving approximately $31 million in federal highway
aid, that the operators of police, fire, and emergency medical
services vehicles are exempt from CDL requirements when operating
these vehicles not only in emergency situations but also pursuant to
their official duties, or activities related to the execution of
emergency governmental functions. Examples of such official duties or
activities include, but are not limited to, training, parades,
funerals, hydrant maintenance, and commercial building inspections.

 PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

New bill.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

None noted, as bill's conformity with federal regulations will
continue to preserve approximately $31 million in federal highway aid.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This act shall take effect immediately.

summary: Allows a person to operate a fire truck without possessing a commercial driver's license.
